title: Clutter in Orbit
context:
Since the launch of Sputnik in 1957, humanity has sent many thousands of satellites into orbit, but only a minority are still working. The rest have joined an expanding cloud of debris that includes spent rocket stages, dead satellites and fragments produced by explosions and collisions. Space agencies track about thirty thousand objects larger than a cricket ball, and statistical models estimate that there are more than a hundred million pieces bigger than a millimetre. Size is misleading, because everything in orbit moves at around seven kilometres per second. At that speed, a fleck of paint can chip a spacecraft window and a bolt can destroy a satellite.

In 1978, the American scientist Donald Kessler proposed that the debris problem could eventually feed on itself. A collision creates fragments, which in turn cause further collisions, until certain orbits become unusable for generations. Fortunately, this chain reaction has not yet occurred, but two events showed how real the danger is. In 2007, a Chinese test destroyed an old weather satellite with a missile, scattering thousands of tracked fragments. Two years later, an American communications satellite and a defunct Russian one collided by accident, the first such collision between two intact satellites. Some altitudes, notably around 800 kilometres, are now thought to be dangerously crowded.

More recently, attention has turned to mega-constellations, networks of thousands of small satellites offering internet access. Their orbits are low, at around 550 kilometres, where the thin upper atmosphere drags dead satellites down within a few years, so the long-term debris risk is smaller than at higher altitudes. Nevertheless, the sheer number of satellites raises the chance of collisions, and astronomers complain that bright trails across the sky are spoiling their images. Operators promise to bring satellites down at the end of their lives, but critics note that a noticeable number have failed soon after launch, and a failed satellite cannot steer itself out of the way.

Avoiding collisions depends on tracking. Radars and telescopes on the ground monitor objects of about ten centimetres and larger, and when a close approach is predicted, the operator may move its satellite out of the way. The International Space Station has done so dozens of times. Such manoeuvres consume fuel and interrupt normal operations, and because the predicted positions of debris are uncertain, many are carried out for encounters that would not actually have led to a collision. Objects too small to be tracked but large enough to cause damage cannot be avoided at all.

Several methods of removal have been suggested, including nets, harpoons, robotic arms and magnets attached to special docking plates. In 2018, a small demonstration mission successfully captured a test target with a net. However, such methods are costly, and the cost of removing a single large object may approach the cost of building a new satellite. There are legal obstacles as well. Under international treaty, a country retains ownership of anything it launches even when it is dead, which means that nobody may remove it without permission.

For these reasons, many experts believe that the priority should be prevention. Existing guidelines advise that satellites be moved out of crowded orbits when their missions end, and that leftover fuel be released so that old rocket stages cannot explode. Compliance, though, is voluntary and uneven. Some economists propose that operators should pay a fee for the right to use busy orbits, which would reward those who keep them clean. Cleaning up is possible in principle, but it is cheaper, and far more effective, not to make the mess in the first place.
